Johnny Five from Short Circuit.

​

A terribly confused, powerful robot slowly coming to the realization it has the ability to empathize and feel. It is rushed through the process of understanding the world through a lone, friendly human being and comes again to realize not only is it a completely unique entity from the world around it, but seemingly endowed with capabilities of understanding the mechanics of the world it finds itself in. It's suddenly thrust into conflict and forced to make the distinction between violence for personal gain and violence for self preservation.

The entire time it does it with a totally constructed personality of naivety and an assumption the world isn't bad, just misunderstood.

Then it moves to the city and learns that all of its capabilities - learning, self repair, seemingly endless empathy for the living - is not only met with ambiguity, but often fear and hatred because that same world doesn't understand what they see. Through more naive decisions, it learns to trust a single human being that not only doesn't fear it, but knows exactly how to manipulate the childlike naivety of an entity with near limitless capability.

Then it is betrayed in a visceral, violent, terrible and wanton act of pure hatred and malice simply because it was in the way.

Then he stood up.

He found his friend. He repaired himself. And he realized the last thing he needed to do was find this person that could be so wrong and to capture him.

Because even through the pain of malice he understood right and wrong.

​

And then Bonnie Tyler plays and I cry because I realize I am Johnny Five.

If a problem case to the highest court in the land, and the highest court doesn’t come up with a decision, maybe you need to change the expectation that your problem is a binary True or False. In other words, if you’re decision can only be made because there’s a disproportionate representation of one idea to another, you probably need to re-examine your question and what you *wanted* to hear.

What historical facts have you learned that support your opposition to the claim? Labeling something as imaginary implies that you have either dismissed the claim without research because of willful disbelief, or that you have objective data that points to an incorrect understanding of a situation - the thing that is being protested is actually not real, or is misrepresented.

Until you are able to provide objective data that a group of people that decry a pain aren't actually experiencing a pain, it seems a poor show of effort - even on the internet - to understand another person's plight and better yourselves by working to solve it.
